original_question: Determine whether there exist two permutation patterns whose avoidance counts switch relative order more than once, and in particular whether two patterns can switch places infinitely often as n grows.
target_in_paper: Section 4, "Are layered patterns the most easily avoided?", especially the discussion on page 248 of Stankova and West [42, Figure 9 and Conjecture 2]: after exhibiting a single reversal in avoidance-count order, the paper asks whether any pair of patterns can switch order twice or more, and records the weaker conjecture that for any pair sigma and tau there exists N such that either Av_sigma(n) < Av_tau(n) for all n > N or Av_sigma(n) > Av_tau(n) for all n > N.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the specific Section 4 phenomenon: comparing avoidance counts of two permutation patterns as n varies, asking whether their relative order can reverse more than once, and highlighting the stronger possibility of infinitely many reversals.
missing_details: The paper is discussing classical permutation patterns; from Section 3 onward it states that, unless otherwise noted, the remainder of the paper concerns classical patterns.
The avoidance-count notation should be made explicit: Av_sigma(n) is the number of permutations of length n that avoid the pattern sigma.
The comparison is made in the Section 4 setting of patterns being "easiest to avoid," so sigma and tau are being compared as patterns of the same fixed length k.

The paper frames the first issue as an existence/nonexistence question: it is unknown whether any pair of patterns exhibits a second switch in relative order, and Stankova and West conjecture that no pair does.

The weaker conjecture should be stated exactly with quantifiers: for any pair sigma, tau there exists an integer N such that either Av_sigma(n) < Av_tau(n) for all n > N, or Av_sigma(n) > Av_tau(n) for all n > N.
The phrase "switch relative order more than once" should be formalized as the sign of Av_sigma(n) - Av_tau(n) changing at least twice as n increases.
The phrase "switch places infinitely often" should be formalized as there being infinitely many n with Av_sigma(n) < Av_tau(n) and infinitely many n with Av_sigma(n) > Av_tau(n).
Because the paper's weaker formulation uses strict inequalities, a fully stand-alone version should either exclude Wilf-equivalent pairs or explicitly say how equality cases are treated.
refined_question: Fix k and let sigma, tau be two non-Wilf-equivalent classical permutation patterns in S_k. If Av_sigma(n) denotes the number of permutations in S_n that avoid sigma, can the inequality between Av_sigma(n) and Av_tau(n) reverse more than once as n increases? More weakly, must there exist an integer N such that either Av_sigma(n) < Av_tau(n) for all n > N or Av_sigma(n) > Av_tau(n) for all n > N; equivalently, can two such patterns switch places infinitely often?
justification: The draft is targeting the specific Section 4 discussion that follows the example Av_53241(n) < Av_43251(n) for 7 <= n <= 12 but Av_53241(13) > Av_43251(13). The paper then says that it is unknown whether such a switch occurs twice or more for any pair of patterns, and immediately records the weaker Stankova-West conjecture that every pair is eventually strictly ordered. The Introduction shows that Section 4 is about comparing patterns by how many permutations of the same length avoid them, Section 3 defines Av_p(n) and fixes the classical-pattern scope for the remainder of the paper, and Section 2 supplies the Wilf-equivalence language needed to make the strict-inequality formulation fully stand-alone.
